questions.prompt: Explain the three DI service lifetimes, which one is the default for web apps, and why DbContext is usually Scoped.

keyPoints.text: Transient gives a fresh instance on every resolution.
Scoped gives one instance per request or scope and is the recommended web default.
keyPoints.quote: one per request / scope (recommended default for web)

keyPoints.text: Singleton gives one instance for the whole application lifetime.
keyPoints.quote: one for the lifetime of the app

keyPoints.text: Scoped services are disposed when their scope ends, which is why DbContext is Scoped.
keyPoints.quote: Scoped services are disposed at the end of the scope — this is why DbContext is usually Scoped.

keyPoints.text: Making everything a Singleton for speed is a production pitfall.
The beginner lesson: AddScoped means a new instance per HTTP request or scope.

questions.prompt: What are captive dependencies and the service locator anti-pattern, and why does the lesson call them hard-to-debug runtime problems?

keyPoints.text: Injecting a Scoped service into a Singleton is the captive dependency case.
It can produce stale data or memory leaks.
keyPoints.quote: This can cause stale data or memory leaks

keyPoints.text: In general: a longer-lived service holds on to a shorter-lived one.
keyPoints.quote: Captive dependencies (longer-lived service holding shorter-lived ones).

keyPoints.text: Pulling services out of IServiceProvider inside classes is the service locator anti-pattern.
keyPoints.quote: Using IServiceProvider as a service locator inside classes.

keyPoints.text: Only the composition root should know concrete implementations.
keyPoints.quote: The composition root is the only place that should know about concrete implementations.

keyPoints.text: Service locators, captive dependencies and wrong lifetimes show up as runtime issues rather than compile errors.

questions.prompt: How does .NET DI handle several implementations of one interface, and how would you extend a service with logging or retry without editing it?

keyPoints.text: Keyed services, new in .NET 8, address multiple implementations of the same interface.
Each implementation is registered under its own key.
A consumer resolves the implementation it needs by key.
A decorator wraps a service, for example with logging, through DI.
keyPoints.quote: Implement a decorator using DI (e.g., logging decorator around a service).

keyPoints.text: The same keyed approach covers multiple payment providers.
keyPoints.quote: Use keyed services to support multiple payment providers.

keyPoints.text: Whatever the design, every implementation still has to be registered.
